st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The measure materially develops the cluster’s governance proposition by translating risk-based, use-context-specific oversight into concrete deployer duties: risk-management programs, impact assessments, annual review, notice, data correction, human-reviewed appeals where feasible, transparency and incident reporting. It also links compliance protection to recognised risk-management frameworks and corrective action. Its contribution is regulatory rather than evidence about legal-task capability or work redesign, and the supplied source is labelled superseded.

st.t: Automated decisions: Notice and recourse remain distinct rights
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s account of the superseded 2024 Colorado framework: it separately specifies consumer notice, data correction and appeal with human review, while combining those rights with deployer risk-governance duties and exclusive attorney-general enforcement. It documents one earlier regulatory design rather than contradicting the cluster’s warning that later frameworks and current legal status require separate checking.

kp.k: Superseded summary records the original enactment and compliance timetable
kp.d: The supplied document is explicitly labelled superseded and presents the bill summary as enacted in 2024. It records approval and effectiveness on May 17, 2024, while specifying February 1, 2026 for the developer and deployer reasonable-care requirements. These are the dates reported by this historical source, not a statement of subsequent law.
qs: SUPERSEDED — Colorado S.B. 24-205: 2024 Automated-Decision-System Enactment
APPROVED** by Governor May 17, 2024  **EFFECTIVE** May 17, 2024
(Note: This summary applies to this bill as enacted.)

kp.k: Developers face reasonable-care duties against algorithmic discrimination
kp.d: From February 1, 2026, the enactment requires developers of high-risk AI systems to use reasonable care against known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination. Compliance with specified provisions creates a rebuttable presumption of reasonable care, rather than an unconditional finding of compliance.
qs: On and after February 1, 2026, the act requires a developer of a high-risk artificial intelligence system (high-risk system) to use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination in the high-risk system.
There is a rebuttable presumption that a developer used reasonable care if the developer complied with specified provisions in the act

kp.k: Developer compliance includes documentation, public transparency and risk reporting
kp.d: The specified developer provisions include disclosures to deployers, documentation supporting impact assessments, and a public statement describing systems and risk management. Developers must disclose specified discrimination risks to the attorney general and known deployers or other developers within 90 days after discovery or receipt of a credible deployer report.
qs: Making available to a deployer of the high-risk system information and documentation necessary to complete an impact assessment of the high-risk system

Making a publicly available statement summarizing the types of high-risk systems that the developer has developed or intentionally and substantially modified and currently makes available to a deployer or other developer and how the developer manages any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination

Disclosing to the attorney general and known deployers or other developers of the high-risk system any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination, within 90 days after the discovery or receipt of a credible report from the deployer, that the high-risk system has caused or is reasonably likely to have caused.

kp.k: Deployers face risk management, impact assessments and annual reviews
kp.d: The enactment also imposes reasonable-care duties on deployers from February 1, 2026, with a rebuttable presumption tied to specified compliance measures. These include a risk management policy and program, impact assessments, and annual deployment reviews to ensure systems are not causing algorithmic discrimination.
qs: The act also, on and after February 1, 2026, requires a deployer of a high-risk system to use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination in the high-risk system.
Implementing a risk management policy and program for the high-risk system
Completing an impact assessment of the high-risk system
Annually reviewing the deployment of each high-risk system deployed by the deployer to ensure that the high-risk system is not causing algorithmic discrimination

kp.k: Consequential decisions trigger notice, correction and appeal protections
kp.d: Specified deployer provisions include notifying consumers when a high-risk system makes or substantially contributes to a consequential decision, allowing correction of incorrect personal data, and allowing appeals of adverse consequential decisions. Human review of appeals is qualified by technical feasibility.
qs: Notifying a consumer of specified items if the high-risk system makes, or will be a substantial factor in making, a consequential decision concerning the consumer
Providing a consumer with an opportunity to correct any incorrect personal data that a high-risk system processed in making a consequential decision

Providing a consumer with an opportunity to appeal, via human review if technically feasible, an adverse consequential decision concerning the consumer arising from the deployment of a high-risk system

kp.k: Deployers must publicly describe systems and report discrimination
kp.d: The specified deployer provisions include public statements about deployed high-risk systems, discrimination-risk management, and the nature, source and extent of information collected and used. Discovery of algorithmic discrimination caused by a system must be disclosed to the attorney general within 90 days.
qs: Making a publicly available statement summarizing the types of high-risk systems that the deployer currently deploys, how the deployer manages any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination that may arise from deployment of each of these high-risk systems, and the nature, source, and extent of the information collected and used by the deployer
Disclosing to the attorney general the discovery of algorithmic discrimination, within 90 days after the discovery, that the high-risk system has caused.

kp.k: Consumer-facing AI requires disclosure of its artificial identity
kp.d: A person doing business in Colorado that deploys or makes available an AI system intended to interact with consumers must disclose that consumers are interacting with AI. The summary states this obligation for consumer-interacting AI systems, rather than limiting it to high-risk systems.
qs: A person doing business in this state, including a deployer or other developer, that deploys or makes available an artificial intelligence system that is intended to interact with consumers must ensure disclosure to each consumer who interacts with the artificial intelligence system that the consumer is interacting with an artificial intelligence system.

kp.k: Specified legal, safety, research and repair activities remain unrestricted
kp.d: The act preserves specified activities, including legal compliance, investigations, immediate protection of life or physical safety, research, recalls and repairs of technical errors impairing functionality. The summary qualifies several categories as specified activities rather than describing unlimited exceptions.
qs: The act does not restrict a developer's, deployer's, or other person's ability to engage in specified activities
Taking immediate steps to protect an interest that is essential for the life or physical safety of a consumer
Conducting and engaging in specified research activities
Effectuating a product recall or repairing technical errors that impair product functionality.

kp.k: Affirmative defense combines recognized frameworks with corrective measures
kp.d: An affirmative defense requires both compliance with a nationally or internationally recognized AI risk management framework designated by the act or attorney general and specified measures to discover and correct violations. Framework compliance alone is not the defense described in the summary.
qs: The act provides an affirmative defense for a developer, deployer, or other person if:

The developer, deployer, or other person involved in a potential violation is in compliance with a nationally or internationally recognized risk management framework for artificial intelligence systems that the act or the attorney general designates
The developer, deployer, or other person takes specified measures to discover and correct violations of the act.

kp.k: Insurance and banking regulation provide conditional compliance pathways
kp.d: Specified insurance entities and developers of AI used by insurers are treated as fully compliant when subject to the identified insurance laws and rules. Listed banks, credit unions, affiliates and subsidiaries receive full-compliance treatment when subject to prudential examination under applicable high-risk-system guidance or regulations meeting the act's criteria.
qs: An insurer, a fraternal benefit society, or a developer of an artificial intelligence system used by an insurer is in full compliance with the act if the entity is subject to specified laws governing insurers' use of external consumer data and information sources, algorithms, and predictive models and rules adopted by the commissioner of insurance.

A bank, out-of-state bank, credit union chartered by the state of Colorado, federal credit union, out-of-state credit union, or any affiliate or subsidiary thereof, is in full compliance with the act if the entity is subject to examination by a state or federal prudential regulator under any published guidance or regulations that apply to the use of high-risk systems and the guidance or regulations meet criteria specified in the act.

kp.k: Attorney general holds exclusive enforcement and rule-making authority
kp.d: The enactment assigns implementation rule-making and exclusive enforcement to the attorney general. Violations constitute deceptive trade practices under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act.
qs: The act grants the attorney general rule-making authority to implement, and exclusive authority to enforce, the requirements of the act.
A person who violates the act engages in a deceptive trade practice pursuant to the "Colorado Consumer Protection Act".

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Colorado General Assembly's enacted-bill summary describes an AI consumer-protection regime, rather than predicting changes to legal services: high-risk AI developers and deployers face reasonable-care duties concerning algorithmic discrimination, and consumer-facing AI requires disclosure.
pts.d: The source states that developers' compliance measures include system disclosures, impact-assessment documentation, public statements and reporting discrimination risks. Deployers' measures include risk-management programs, impact assessments, annual reviews, consumer notices, data correction and opportunities to appeal adverse consequential decisions through human review where technically feasible. Compliance with specified provisions creates rebuttable presumptions of reasonable care. The attorney general has rule-making and exclusive enforcement authority, and violations constitute deceptive trade practices. These are descriptions of the 2024 enactment's requirements, not empirical claims that AI reduces costs, displaces lawyers or improves outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is legislative authority: an official Colorado General Assembly summary of SB24-205 as enacted, supported by its enactment history.
pts.d: The page identifies the measure as having become law, records the governor's signature on May 17, 2024, and lists the signed act and session-law entry. It supplies no empirical data, AI benchmarks, discrimination case studies or measured effects of the safeguards. Its evidence supports what the 2024 enactment provides, not a demonstrated reduction in discrimination or any forecast of legal-market effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes the May 17, 2024 enactment/effective date from the February 1, 2026 start specified for high-risk-system duties; the supplied document is explicitly marked superseded.
pts.d: These dates describe the historical 2024 enactment, not verified current law; the document does not supply the superseding provisions. Developer risk disclosures are due within 90 days of discovery or receipt of a credible deployer report, while deployer disclosures to the attorney general are due within 90 days of discovering discrimination caused by a system. Deployment reviews are annual. Human review of appeals is qualified by technical feasibility. The summary describes an affirmative defense conditioned on both compliance with a designated recognized AI risk-management framework and specified discovery-and-correction measures. It also describes conditional deemed compliance for certain insurance and banking entities under qualifying sectoral oversight, and preserves specified activities such as legal compliance, investigations, safety measures, research and repairs.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated affected groups are AI developers and deployers, consumers, businesses offering consumer-interacting AI, sectorally regulated insurance and banking entities, and the Colorado attorney general.
pts.d: Developers must support downstream assessment and communicate risks; deployers must manage and assess deployment risks and provide consumer-facing safeguards. Consumers affected by consequential decisions receive notice, correction and appeal opportunities, while people interacting with consumer-facing AI receive disclosure. Certain insurance and banking entities can satisfy the act through qualifying sectoral regulation. The attorney general implements and exclusively enforces the requirements. The source does not identify law firms, lawyers, ALSPs or legal departments as separately affected groups, or claim effects on their employment, pricing or service delivery.
